takes.take: Most multi-agent systems are context management in disguise.
takes.for: The measurable wins come from giving each sub-task a clean, focused context and from reading in parallel. The “team of agents” framing adds little beyond that, and it multiplies tokens.
takes.against: Separation also changes behavior. An independent reviewer catches errors that one long context rationalizes away, and parallel exploration finds options a single trajectory never tries.

takes.take: You don’t need a framework; you need a while loop.
takes.for: The agent loop is about fifty lines. Frameworks hide prompts, make debugging opaque and churn their APIs faster than you can upgrade.
takes.against: Durable execution, tracing, streaming, retries, human approvals and multi-provider support are real work. A mature framework encodes production lessons you would otherwise relearn the hard way.

takes.take: RAG is dead; long context killed it.
takes.for: With million-token windows and prompt caching, putting the whole corpus in the prompt is simpler and never suffers a retrieval miss.
takes.against: Cost and latency grow with context, quality degrades with distractors, corpora outgrow any window, and permissions and freshness need a retrieval step anyway.

takes.take: Fine-tuning is usually a mistake for application teams.
takes.for: Prompting, retrieval and evals deliver most of the wins, and a fine-tune pins you to an old base model while the frontier moves.
takes.against: For narrow, high-volume tasks a fine-tuned small model can be cheaper, faster and more consistent, and reinforcement fine-tuning can teach behavior no prompt reliably produces.

takes.take: LLM judges are vibes with extra steps.
takes.for: Uncalibrated judges carry position, verbosity and self-preference biases, and they drift when the judge model changes.
takes.against: A judge checked against human labels on one specific, binary criterion is a measurement instrument with known error rates. It scales review that humans cannot.

takes.for: Modern models follow plain instructions, and optimizers plus context engineering matter more than clever phrasing.
takes.against: Specifying a task clearly never dies. The work moved from tricks to writing good specs, examples and tool descriptions, and those still swing results by wide margins.

takes.take: Benchmarks are broken, so ignore leaderboards.
takes.for: Saturation, contamination and tuning to a benchmark’s format make public scores poor predictors of your use case.
takes.against: Well-built benchmarks still track coarse capability trends, and fresh held-out ones catch regressions. The fix is reading them critically, not ignoring them.

takes.take: Better models will solve prompt injection.
takes.for: Models keep improving at telling instructions from data, and adversarial training hardens them further.
takes.against: While instructions and data share one channel, a capable attacker finds a phrasing that works some of the time. Reliable defenses remove capabilities rather than asking the model to behave.

takes.take: Vibe-coded software is fine for production if the tests pass.
takes.for: Tests define behavior. If they pass, it should not matter who or what wrote the code.
takes.against: Tests cover what someone thought to test. Unreviewed code accumulates security holes, duplicated logic and design debt that no test suite catches.

takes.for: High-quality pretraining text is finite, the returns per order of magnitude of compute look smaller, and training costs keep ballooning.
takes.against: New axes keep appearing: RL post-training, test-time compute, synthetic data and better architectures. Measured capabilities kept rising through 2025 and 2026.

takes.take: Every agent should start life as a workflow.
takes.for: Fixed code paths are cheaper, testable and predictable, and most tasks people call agentic have known steps.
takes.against: Open-ended tasks with unknown steps, such as coding and research, are exactly where agents beat workflows. Forcing them into fixed branches produces brittle software.

takes.take: MCP is function calling with extra ceremony.
takes.for: For one app calling its own functions, MCP adds a process boundary and a protocol for no gain.
takes.against: The value is the N×M problem: one server works in every compliant host with standard discovery, auth and consent. For purely internal functions, a plain function is indeed fine.
